chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Charlie Barnet's band members and Horace's originals for him
summary: Barnet, an Ellington admirer who liked 'mistakes', had Cliff Leeman, Bill Miller, Bernie Privin, Spot Esposito and Eddie Sauter. Horace wrote originals like 'Charleston Alley' and 'Ponce de Leon'.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: And Charlie Barnett was another guy like that, and I think we mentioned something like this before, that I made a couple of mistakes where it should have been a B flat, and I had a B natural, and one of those things, I said, 'Oh, man, this is wrong, this is dischord.' And Charlie said, 'You remember what you did?' I says, 'Yeah. I made a mistake.' 'Keep it in. Keep it in,' one of those things. He liked weird things like that. Of course, he was a fan, as you know, a great admirer of Duke Ellington. He patterned quite a few things after Duke. But this is what happened to those chords and things
Who were some of the people on Charlie Barnett's band when you were writing?
Charlie had quite a few great musicians in his band. At the time that I was with him, you know, he had a drummer named Cliff Leeman.

And here in Denver here a few weeks back I think he was playing with Peanuts Hucko for a while, and then there was as a change, and, well, Cliff's pretty well up there now, but he was more or less swinging the band at that time. I haven't heard his style recently.
I heard him about two years ago. He's been with the Jazz Party at Dick Gibson's.

Well, he was in that Charlie Barnett Band, and there was a great pianist in that band named Bill Miller, and I think he's out to MGM now. Man, he could play. He was a quiet little guy, and he could write. Oh, man, he could write like mad. And he had a trumpet player named Bernie Priven. I think it's P-r-i-v-e-n, I think; man, he could play. And he had a first trumpet player, a little short guy named Spots Esposito, we called him, you know.
And I tell you another great trumpet player and great arranger that was in that band, and I know you know him, Eddie Sauter.

Eddie Sauter Sotter was in that band. Man, that little guy could write like mad, and in the beginning he didn't write anything, but as time went on, man, he's -- you know the story (unintelligible) on it now. And he's a wonderful guy, and I haven't seen him in years, but these are the type of musicians that Charlie had surrounded himself with.
Did you write originals for him or --

Yeah, I wrote some originals for him, like "Charleston Alley" and "Ponce de Leon" and a thing called "that" (unintelligible). Of course, Charlie named some of these things, you know, for me. He was good at that. He had a little publishing company in the Paramount Theater Building in New York during that time. Nothing too much happened because he was doing one nighters, and he had an attorney that was representing him, was in charge of the music publishing company, but it was a lot of fun, though.
